--- title: "[Graph.percolation_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute percolation centrality for all nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L25463-L25607){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.percolation_centrality( states=None, weight=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Percolation centrality](/assets/graphs/percolation-centrality.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared seven-node graph with the two percolated nodes, A and G, outlined; every other node has state 0. Only paths that start at A or G count, so the nodes linking A to G matter most: E and F share the top at 0.60, then C 0.50, with B and D 0.05 and the endpoints A and G 0." width="100%"} Percolation centrality (Piraveenan et al., 2013) measures the importance of nodes based on the proportion of 'percolated paths' that pass through them. Every node carries a percolation state between `0.0` and `1.0` (e.g., how infected, informed, or compromised it is), and shortest paths are weighted by the state of the node they start from. A node scores highly when it lies on many shortest paths leading *out of* highly percolated nodes, so it is the natural relay for whatever those nodes are spreading. This is particularly useful for: - finding the nodes best placed to pass on an infection or rumor from the nodes that already carry it - prioritizing interventions (vaccination, patching, monitoring) given the current state of an outbreak - re-ranking betweenness as a spreading process evolves, by recomputing with updated states When every node has the same state (the default is `1.0` for all), the score reduces to standard normalized betweenness centrality. All shortest paths are counted by number of hops and, for directed graphs, follow edge direction. Like betweenness, the computation runs a shortest-path search from every node, so it can be slow on large graphs. Note that, unlike most centrality methods, the returned dictionary is keyed by node *label* rather than node ID. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [states]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[int, float] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Dictionary mapping node labels to percolation states, each between `0.0` and `1.0`. Keys are matched against node labels as strings (an integer key `1` matches the label `"1"`), and an unknown label raises a `ValueError`. Nodes missing from the dictionary get a state of `1.0`, so to mark only a few nodes as percolated you must give the others an explicit `0.0`. If `None` (default), every node has state `1.0` and the result equals normalized betweenness centrality. If the states sum to `1.0` or less (e.g., a single fully percolated node), every score is `0.0`. [weight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of an edge attribute holding weights. Accepted for API compatibility but currently has no effect: path lengths are always counted in hops. Defaults to `None`. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name used to store the scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), the column is named `"percolation_centrality"`. An existing column with the same name is overwritten. Only used when `return_dict=` is `False`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the scores as a dictionary keyed by node label and leave the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), store the scores in the node DataFrame under `attr_name=` and return the graph for method chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node labels (or node IDs, for nodes without a label) to percolation centrality values. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): the graph itself, with the scores stored as a node attribute. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a key in `states=` does not match any node label, or if a state lies outside `[0.0, 1.0]`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below is a five-node line A to E with a two-node branch (F, G) hanging off C. With the default states, every node is equally percolated and the scores are simply normalized betweenness: C, the junction, is highest. ::: {#5fc28f00 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("C", "F"), ("F", "G")]) ) graph.percolation_centrality(return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'G': 0.0, 'C': 0.8, 'A': 0.0, 'E': 0.0, 'F': 0.33333333333333337, 'D': 0.33333333333333337, 'B': 0.33333333333333337} ``` ::: ::: Now suppose only A and G are infected. Paths that start at those two nodes are the only ones that count, so B and F (the first hops out of the infected nodes) climb from `0.33` to `0.6`, while D, which only carries traffic toward the uninfected end E, drops to `0.2`. Every other node must be given an explicit state of `0.0`: ::: {#a83c933b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} states = {"A": 1.0, "G": 1.0, "B": 0.0, "C": 0.0, "D": 0.0, "E": 0.0, "F": 0.0} graph.percolation_centrality(states=states, return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'G': 0.0, 'C': 0.8, 'A': 0.0, 'E': 0.0, 'F': 0.6000000000000001, 'D': 0.2, 'B': 0.6000000000000001} ``` ::: ::: With `return_dict=False` (the default) the scores go into the node DataFrame, here under a custom column name: ::: {#edc850ab .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.percolation_centrality(states=states, attr_name="spread_risk") graph.get_node_df().select(["label", "spread_risk"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
